prompt: A home NAT router rewrites a packet's source IP from 192.168.1.20 to its public address, and its source port too. Why must it also update the **TCP** checksum, even though the TCP payload hasn't changed?

options.text: Because the TCP checksum covers a pseudo-header that includes the source and destination IP addresses, as well as the TCP header with its ports
options.explanation: Correct. Addresses and TCP ports are checksum inputs, so translation must maintain the checksum by adjustment or recomputation. Some numerical changes can cancel, leaving the checksum value unchanged.

options.text: Because the TTL changed and TCP checksums cover the TTL
options.explanation: The TTL is not part of the TCP pseudo-header. The TTL change only affects the IPv4 header checksum.

options.text: It doesn't need to; TCP checksums only cover TCP data
options.explanation: TCP includes a pseudo-header and its own header as well as data. Ignoring changed checksum inputs can cause validation failure.

options.text: Because the Ethernet FCS is copied into the TCP header
options.explanation: The FCS is a link-layer trailer recomputed on every hop. It is never copied into TCP.

workedExample: TCP covers its IP pseudo-header, TCP header and data. Translation changes some of these inputs. The translator must maintain a valid checksum, usually through incremental adjustment or recomputation. It need not become numerically different for every possible pair of changes.

prompt: Why does QUIC run over UDP rather than being a new transport protocol with its own IP protocol number, alongside TCP (6) and UDP (17)?

options.text: Because UDP provides the reliability that QUIC needs
options.explanation: UDP provides no reliability at all. QUIC implements its own acknowledgements, retransmission and congestion control on top.

options.text: Because IP has no spare protocol numbers left
options.explanation: IP protocol numbers are not exhausted. The relevant concern is support by deployed networks and endpoints.

options.text: UDP improves deployability through existing endpoint APIs and many NATs and firewalls compared with an unfamiliar IP transport protocol
options.explanation: Correct. This is not universal reachability: some networks block UDP or QUIC. QUIC protects packet contents and selected header fields; it does not encrypt every header field.

options.text: Because the operating system kernel can only send TCP or UDP
options.explanation: Kernels can send arbitrary IP protocols (SCTP exists, for example). Being in user space is a bonus of UDP, but the main reason is what the network lets through.

workedExample: A new IP transport number can require middlebox and endpoint support. UDP provides an already supported transport substrate in many environments, making deployment easier. QUIC adds transport and security functionality above UDP. Its protected contents and selected protected header fields reduce some ossification risks, while fields such as connection IDs remain visible. Neither UDP reachability nor freedom from ossification is guaranteed.

prompt: A VXLAN tunnel must fit an inner Ethernet frame inside UDP and an outer IP packet. The underlay's IP MTU is unchanged. Why can a tenant's previously valid full-size IP packet become too large?

options.text: The tunnel headers use no space inside the outer IP packet
options.explanation: Outer IP, UDP and VXLAN headers occupy part of that packet budget.

options.text: Only the outer Ethernet FCS reduces the outer IP MTU
options.explanation: The outer Ethernet header and FCS sit outside the outer IP packet's MTU budget.

options.text: Tunnel headers and the inner Ethernet header consume part of the outer IP-packet budget
options.explanation: Correct. The tenant's IP packet shares that outer budget with encapsulation that was absent before.

options.text: The tenant's TCP port number gets wider inside VXLAN
options.explanation: VXLAN encapsulates the frame; it does not widen transport port fields.

workedExample: Draw the nesting: outer Ethernet contains outer IP, which contains UDP, VXLAN and the inner Ethernet frame. The underlay IP MTU limits the entire outer IP packet. The tenant's IP packet is only part of that budget. Check a sufficient underlay MTU or reduce the tenant MTU; unresolved fragmentation or path-MTU adaptation can otherwise cause size-dependent failure.

link.title: RFC 7348: Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN)

prompt: Which examples show interaction across layers or an intermediate system processing higher-layer information? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wi-Fi link retries can recover radio losses before TCP sees them and responds with congestion control
options.explanation: Correct. This is a cross-layer performance interaction, but retries also serve other protocols and do not exist solely because of TCP.

options.text: A load balancer reads the HTTP Host header to choose a backend
options.explanation: Correct. An application proxy processes layer-7 information. That does not itself prove ossification or violate the layering model.

options.text: The IP layer needs to know the link's MTU to size its packets
options.explanation: Correct. MTU is a link service property used by IP. Depending on IP version and policy, an oversized packet can be fragmented, rejected or dropped; such an interface is not inherently a design flaw.

options.text: HTTP/2 was deployed without any changes to Ethernet
options.explanation: That's the opposite: layering *working* as intended. Ethernet carries whatever payload it is given.

workedExample: Link retries affect what TCP observes; an HTTP proxy processes application messages in the path; and IP uses the MTU exposed by its link interface. All are interactions to consider when reasoning across layers. HTTP/2 changing independently of Ethernet illustrates separation of responsibilities. Cross-layer interaction is not automatically a violation or a bug.
